title: Waves and Sound
seo_title: Grade 11 Physics (SPH3U): Waves and Sound Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: Transverse and longitudinal waves; frequency, period, wavelength and the universal wave equation; the speed of sound; interference, standing waves and resonance in strings and air columns; beats and the Doppler effect. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Physics, Grade 11, University Preparation (SPH3U), Strand E: Waves and Sound)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Physics (SPH3U) worksheets on waves and sound: wave properties, the wave equation, the speed of sound, echoes, interference, standing waves, resonance in air columns and beats. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Speed of sound in air ≈ 332 + 0.6T m/s.
body_html:
How to think about it

A wave carries energy without carrying matter. Transverse waves vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel; longitudinal waves (like sound) vibrate along it. The universal wave equation is v = fλ, and the period T = 1 ÷ f.

The speed of sound in air is about 332 m/s at 0 °C and rises by about 0.6 m/s for each degree. When waves overlap they interfere; standing waves form in strings and air columns at resonant frequencies. Two close frequencies give beats at fbeat = |f₁ − f₂|.

Example

A wave has f = 50 Hz and λ = 4.0 m. Speed?

v = fλ = 50 × 4.0

Answer: 200 m/s

Example

Two tuning forks: 440 Hz and 444 Hz. Beat frequency?

|444 − 440|

Answer: 4 Hz

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a higher frequency means a faster wave in the same medium: the wavelength gets shorter instead.
  • Forgetting to halve the time for an echo (the sound goes there and back).
  • Saying sound can travel through a vacuum.

faq.q: Why does sound travel faster in warm air?
faq.a: The air particles move faster, so they pass the vibration on more quickly.
